name: Bonepulling

card.summary: A manual practice of applying sustained force to the palate or facial bones, promoted online as a way to reshape the midface and jaw toward a more forward, defined look.
card.aka: bone pulling, thumbpulling, progressive stress exercises
card.note: Force applied to teeth, jaw joints and the neck can cause injury; orthodontists describe supervised appliances, not hand pulling, as the method for moving facial structures.

quick.overview:
Bonepulling is a do-it-yourself practice in which a person uses their hands, usually the thumbs, to apply steady force to part of the face, most often the palate, in the hope of nudging the upper jaw forward or wider. Followers aim for a more projected midface, broader palate and stronger facial structure.

Proponents compare it to orthodontic appliances, which also apply slow, constant force, and argue that bone adapts to loading. Orthodontists and craniofacial specialists describe appliances and surgery, supervised by clinicians, as the established routes to moving facial bones, and no published trial has tested manual bonepulling.
quick.how: Guides circulating on looksmax.org describe bonepulling as a series of sessions using thumb pressure on the soft palate, with variations in direction (forward, lateral and reverse) and cushioning or head support to spread the force. Followers describe it as a long-term routine, usually combined with tongue-posture practices such as mewing.
quick.risks: Risks that clinicians associate with unsupervised force on the mouth and face include tooth loosening or movement, gum and palate injury, jaw-joint strain and neck strain. Guides themselves warn against pushing on teeth and recommend head support. No published trial shows that hand pulling changes adult facial bones.

lead: Bonepulling (also written bone pulling, and related to thumbpulling and progressive-stress exercises) is a practice in looksmaxxing communities in which a person applies sustained manual force to facial structures, most commonly the palate, to try to change facial bone position. The goal followers state is a more forward, wider or more projected midface and jaw, which they associate with a more defined, attractive face.[1][2]

Its rationale, as laid out in a multi-part guide series on looksmax.org, rests on mechanotransduction: the idea that bone and muscle adapt to mechanical stress, as seen with orthodontic appliances that apply slow, steady force.[2] Proponents argue that hand-applied force could work in a similar way and describe it as a no-cost counterpart to braces and palatal expanders.[2] The concept draws on the long-standing principle, often called Wolff's law, that bone remodels in response to load.[8]

Orthodontists move teeth and widen jaws with clinician-supervised appliances and, in adults whose palatal suture has fused, with surgical or mini-implant-assisted methods.[7] No published human study has tested manual bonepulling. Related claims about tongue posture (mewing) are described by Wikipedia as unproven, with experts quoted as saying no credible research has shown the approach changes jaw structure.[3] Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing places such facial-structure practices in the 'softmaxxing' versus 'hardmaxxing' vocabulary of the community and notes press coverage from outlets including The Guardian, the BBC and The New York Times.[6]

angle.text: Followers use bonepulling to try to move the upper jaw forward or expand the palate, aiming for a more projected midface. They frame it as the DIY counterpart of orthodontic appliances, which also work by steady force.

paras: Bonepulling guides describe pulling or pushing against the palate with the thumbs, with the stated aim of encouraging palate expansion and forward growth of the maxilla.[1] One guide specifies pulling against the soft palate at the back of the mouth rather than against the teeth, and says teeth move as a consequence of palate expansion.[1] It also advises cushioning for the thumbs and leaning the head on a wall or shelf so that neck and spine do not bear the force.[1] Variants named in the series include forward, lateral and reverse directions.[1]

The wider vocabulary of looksmaxxing came from incel-era message boards in the 2010s, including PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net, and reached TikTok in the early 2020s, according to sources summarised on Wikipedia.[6] Bonepulling does not have a Wikipedia article of its own; it circulates mainly in forum guides. The two guides in the series on looksmax.org, titled 'Primal Revolution' parts 11 and 12, were posted in 2024 and set out a theory section followed by a description of forward, lateral and reverse pulling.[1][2]

Earlier forum threads on related ideas date to 2020, including a thread asking whether bone pulling could move an over-projected midface backwards, where members compared the idea with surgery.[4] The practice sits beside mewing, which entered mainstream attention from January 2019 and was popularised by orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike Mew.[3] Mike Mew was struck from the UK dental register in 2024, according to Wikipedia.[3]

The opening guide in the series argues that orthodontic appliances produce change through slow, consistent, progressive stress, and that bone, muscle and fat adapt to force via mechanotransduction, in which osteocytes sense strain and trigger remodelling.[2] Followers apply this to manual force, describing it as a no-cost counterpart to braces and palatal expanders.[2]
Forum members also discuss related ideas, such as using belts or straps to try to move parts of the midface back, which other members in the thread treated as speculative.[4]

The guide series presents bonepulling as a non-surgical way to target facial structure, as a long-term routine, and alongside tongue-posture practice; its stated aim is palate expansion and forward maxillary growth.[1][2]

Published literature on bone anchors and orthopaedic fixation concerns surgical hardware and does not address manual facial force.[5] Orthodontists use controlled appliances placed and monitored by clinicians, and craniofacial surgeons use procedures such as Le Fort osteotomies to reposition the midface.[4] The wider oral-posture movement is described on Wikipedia as an unproven form of training, with a 2019 paper in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery quoted as saying no credible research has proven orthotropics effective.[3]

Wolff's law, formulated by the German surgeon Julius Wolff in the 19th century, holds that bone remodels to the loads placed on it; present-day accounts describe remodelling as driven by osteocytes sensing strain, and note that the effect depends on the duration, magnitude and rate of loading, with cyclic loading associated with bone formation.[8] Proponents cite this process in support of progressive-stress exercises.[2]

Orthodontic literature describes palatal expansion as a clinician-controlled process. Wikipedia's account says expanders are most often used in children and adolescents aged roughly 8 to 18, that they work by separating the two halves of the maxilla along the mid-palatal suture, that after puberty the suture typically fuses and must be surgically opened or bypassed with mini-implant-assisted devices, and that treatment begun after the growth spurt produces mostly dental rather than skeletal change.[7] Reported side effects of supervised expansion include pain, speech changes, gaps between the front teeth and thinning of bone on the cheek side of teeth.[7] Orthodontic tooth movement is delivered by specialists who adjust appliances every 4 to 10 weeks, and relapse is common, with retainers usually advised.[9]

The guides themselves note risks that they try to manage, such as protecting thumbs, avoiding force on teeth and supporting the head to spare neck ligaments.[1] Dental professionals generally associate uncontrolled force on teeth with movement, loosening and gum injury, and jaw-joint strain is a recognised concern with repeated loading.

Facial surgeons quoted in coverage of related looksmaxxing practices such as bonesmashing warn of fractures, nerve and vessel injury and facial misalignment; these warnings concern striking the face and are listed here as context for hard-force practices, not as findings about bonepulling.[6] Pulling-specific risks are discussed in clinical terms only by analogy to appliance side effects.[7]

Within looksmax.org, bonepulling sits among 'bonehack' practices and is discussed with enthusiasm and scepticism alike; some replies in the guide threads joke that members would sooner put their thumbs in their mouths than get braces, which shows the tension between do-it-yourself and clinician-led routes.[2] The guide author advises cushioning and head support, which indicates that the guide itself addresses injury.[1]
Researchers writing in 2025 (Konig, Sidhu and Corpuz, cited on Wikipedia) advise physicians to help patients distinguish safe looksmaxxing practices from harmful ones.[6]

timeline.event: Emerson Angell publishes the first paper on palatal expansion in Dental Cosmos, per Wikipedia's account. [7]
Julius Wolff's treatise on bone transformation, source of 'Wolff's law', is published. [8]
Mewing attention rises sharply on social media, within looksmaxxing and incel communities. [3]
Forum thread on whether bone pulling could move the midface backwards. [4]
'Primal Revolution' guide parts 11 and 12 on bonepulling and progressive-stress exercises are posted on looksmax.org. [1][2]
Mike Mew is struck from the UK dental register. [3]
Konig, Sidhu and Corpuz advise physicians on separating safe from harmful looksmaxxing practices. [6]

lore.intro: Bonepulling is discussed on looksmax.org in a multi-part guide series on progressive stress, alongside other bonehack practices.[2]

claims.claim: Sustained hand pressure on the palate can expand the palate and move the maxilla forward
claims.believers: Guide authors compare it to orthodontic force and cite mechanotransduction, saying bone adapts to slow progressive stress.[1][2]
claims.experts: No published study has tested manual bonepulling; orthodontic movement is described in the clinical literature using supervised appliances.[3]

claims.claim: Strap or belt pressure could move an overprojected midface backward
claims.believers: A forum poster proposed wrapping a belt around the midface, while rating the odds as low.[4]
claims.experts: Surgical repositioning of the midface is done with osteotomies by surgeons, not external straps.[4]

claims.claim: Bone adapts to progressive stress, so hand pressure can reshape the face like braces do
claims.believers: The guide series cites mechanotransduction and orthodontic appliances as proof of concept.[2]
claims.experts: Wolff's law is accepted for bone loading generally, but orthodontic expansion in the literature uses controlled appliances, and adult sutures typically fuse.[7][8]

claims.claim: Pulling should be done on the soft palate, not the teeth, because teeth move as a result of expansion
claims.believers: The part 12 guide states the placement and the head-support and cushioning measures.[1]
claims.experts: Orthodontic texts describe force on teeth and bone as something specialists monitor; no study has measured the placement claim.[7][9]

claims.claim: It works best combined with mewing
claims.believers: Followers present tongue posture and pulling as complementary.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes mewing as unproven and quotes experts that no credible research shows it changes jaw structure.[3]

claims.claim: Bonepulling is a safe free alternative to surgery
claims.believers: Guide authors describe it as low-cost and note protective steps.[1]
claims.experts: Clinicians associate unsupervised force on teeth with loosening and gum injury and the guides themselves warn about neck strain; no safety study exists.[1][7]
